title: Design cache
summary: Design a bounded, thread-safe cache with O(1) LRU eviction and TTL — HashMap plus doubly-linked list, done right under concurrency.

blocks.title: What the interviewer is really testing
blocks.text: This is not a **HashMap exercise**. Anyone can write `get` and `put`. The real test is: **can you hold four invariants at once under concurrency — O(1) lookup, O(1) eviction, bounded memory, and no stale reads — without corrupting the list?** If you reach for `LinkedHashMap` and `synchronized`, you pass the easy version and fail the Hard version. They want to see you choose the structure that survives LRU promotion on read, lazy TTL expiry, and a thundering herd on miss.
The problem

Design an in-memory, bounded, thread-safe cache. It stores key-value pairs up to a fixed capacity, evicts the least-recently-used entry when full, supports per-entry time-to-live, and stays correct when dozens of threads hammer `get` and `put` concurrently. You must get O(1) average `get` and `put`, exact capacity enforcement, and no unbounded background work. The cache is a library, not a distributed system: one process, one instance, but it must be built so eviction policy and loading logic can be swapped without rewriting the core.

items: `V get(K key)` — return value if present and not expired, else `null`. A successful `get` counts as a use and promotes the entry to most-recently-used.
`void put(K key, V value)` — insert or overwrite. Overwrite counts as a use. If over capacity after insert, evict LRU.
`void put(K key, V value, long ttlMillis)` — same as above but entry expires `ttlMillis` after write. `ttl <= 0` means no expiry.
`void remove(K key)` and `void clear()` — explicit invalidation.
`int size()` — number of live entries. Must not count expired-but-not-yet-cleaned entries as live for capacity decisions.

blocks.text: Clarify before you code

Do not write a line until you lock these answers. The interviewer changes the difficulty by changing these assumptions, and guessing wrong forces a rewrite in front of them. Ask in this order, state your default if they say you choose.

items.title: What is capacity — entries or bytes?
items.text: Entries is the interview default and what LRU assumes. Bytes or weight requires a `weigher` function and makes eviction loop until weight fits, not just one eviction. Agree on entries unless they push you.

items.title: Is LRU fixed or pluggable?
items.text: If they say LRU only, hard-wire the doubly-linked list. If they hint LFU, FIFO, or custom, extract an `EvictionPolicy` interface now. Retrofitting it later breaks your locking.

items.title: Do reads mutate state?
items.text: Yes for LRU — `get` reorders the list. This kills any plan to use a read-write lock with concurrent reads. Say it out loud: LRU reads are writes. That one sentence earns trust.

items.title: TTL semantics — lazy, active, or both?
items.text: Lazy expiry on access is mandatory and cheap. Active background cleaning is optional and dangerous. Agree that expired entries are treated as missing on `get`, and capacity reclaims them on `put`. Only add a cleaner thread if they demand strict memory bounds.

items.title: Miss handling — who loads the database?
items.text: Dumb cache just returns null. Smart cache takes a `CacheLoader` and does read-through. This decides whether you need singleflight to prevent thundering herd. Ask: can two threads load the same missing key at once?

rows: Bounded capacity on entry count, exact enforcement
Unbounded cache is a memory leak with an API
LRU eviction + overwrite promotes to MRU
Per-key TTL, lazy expiry on read and write path
Expiry without a timer thread is the expected trade-off
remove, clear, size with live-entry semantics
Size lying about expired entries fails hidden tests
Rules out scans, TreeMap, or global queue search
Thread-safe with no lost updates or broken list
The Hard part; list corruption is the classic fail
Eviction policy behind interface, loader injectable
Lets you answer LFU and read-through follow-ups without rewrite

blocks.text: Approach 1 — the naive HashMap

The obvious start is `HashMap<K,V>` plus `HashMap<K,Long>` for timestamps, guarded by `synchronized`. On `put` when full, scan all keys to find the oldest timestamp and remove it. On `get`, check timestamp and return null if expired. It passes a single-threaded demo in three minutes, which is exactly why interviewers let you write it — then they break it.

This fails on three axes, and you should name all three before the interviewer does. First, **eviction is O(N)** — every insert over capacity scans the whole access map. At 100k entries that scan dominates throughput. Trade-off: you saved pointer complexity and paid linear write cost. Second, **global `synchronized` serialises everything** — 32 reader threads queue behind one writer even though HashMap reads could overlap. Throughput collapses exactly when a cache should help most. Third, **TTL is bolted on, not designed in** — you need a third map for expiry, lazy checks scattered in two methods, and no story for who reclaims expired entries for capacity. The structure cannot evolve to LFU, weighted eviction, or loader-based singleflight because ordering, storage, and locking are tangled in one class. Throw it away, but keep the lesson: ordering metadata must be O(1) updatable.
The real design: map plus intrusive LRU list

The correct core is two structures sharing the same `Node` objects: a `HashMap<K, Node>` for O(1) lookup and a doubly-linked list with dummy head and tail for O(1) promotion and eviction. `Node` holds key, value, `expiryAt`, and `prev/next`. MRU sits right after head, LRU sits right before tail. `get` finds the node, checks expiry, unlinks and re-links it at head, returns value. `put` either updates in place and promotes, or creates a node, inserts at head, and while over capacity unlinks from tail. Expiry is **lazy**: expired is missing. No timer, no scan on read. One lock guards both structures together because they are one invariant — map and list must move atomically. Splitting locks between them is how lists get corrupted. Trade-off stated plainly: you pay two extra pointers per entry and manual pointer code to buy guaranteed O(1) eviction and no background thread.

blocks.title: Request flow
blocks.caption: Every path maintains map-plus-list consistency under one lock.
blocks.code:
graph TD
  A[Client] --> B[get or put]
  B --> C{hit and fresh}
  C -->|yes| D[promote to MRU and return]
  C -->|expired| E[treat as miss unlink node]
  C -->|miss| F[load or accept value]
  E --> F
  F --> G[insert at MRU head]
  G --> H{over capacity}
  H -->|yes| I[evict LRU from tail]
  H -->|no| J[return]
  I --> J

blocks.text: Why this shape and not the alternatives. Versus `LinkedHashMap` with `removeEldestEntry`: that class already does map-plus-list, and in production you should use it or Caffeine. In an interview you must hand-roll the list, because the interviewer cannot see your pointer reasoning otherwise. Say that explicitly — production versus interview trade-off. Versus `ConcurrentHashMap` plus `ConcurrentLinkedQueue`: the queue cannot remove from the middle in O(1) on `get`, so promotion becomes O(N) or leaves duplicates that need garbage handling. That design is only valid for FIFO, never LRU. Versus active TTL with a `ScheduledExecutor`: it gives strict memory reclamation but adds a thread, lock contention on every tick, and shutdown lifecycle you must test. Lazy expiry plus opportunistic reclaim on `put` gives amortised O(1) with zero threads. Choose lazy unless they demand a hard memory ceiling, then add a bounded cleaner that only trims the tail, never scans.
Structure at runtime

blocks.title: Class structure
blocks.caption: Storage, ordering, and policy are separate; one lock owns the invariant.

blocks.text: Three roles, one owner. `LRUCache` owns the lock and the invariant; `Node` is dumb storage with pointers; `EvictionPolicy` and `CacheLoader` are seams for follow-ups. Do not let the policy hold its own lock — it is called with the cache lock held and must be non-blocking and non-reentrant. Do not call `CacheLoader.load` while holding the lock, or you turn a 50ms database stall into a global cache stall and invite deadlock if the loader calls back into the cache. The pattern is: check under lock, load outside lock, re-check and install under lock. That double-check is the difference between a cache and a bottleneck.
Working code

Below is the version to write on a whiteboard. Single `ReentrantLock`, dummy head and tail so unlink logic has no null branches, expiry checked in one helper. `get` promotes, which is why it takes the write lock — say that while writing. Production would shard or use Caffeine; this is the interview-optimal point between clarity and correctness.

blocks.code:
import threading, time
from collections import OrderedDict
from typing import Optional

class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        assert capacity > 0
        self.capacity = capacity
        self._data: OrderedDict = OrderedDict()  # key -> (value, expiry)
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def get(self, key):
        with self._lock:
            if key not in self._data:
                return None
            value, exp = self._data.pop(key)
            if exp != float("inf") and time.time() >= exp:
                return None  # lazy expiry: do not reinsert
            self._data[key] = (value, exp)  # promote to MRU
            return value

    def put(self, key, value, ttl_ms: int = 0):
        exp = float("inf") if ttl_ms <= 0 else time.time() + ttl_ms / 1000.0
        with self._lock:
            if key in self._data:
                self._data.pop(key)
            self._data[key] = (value, exp)
            # reclaim expired tail opportunistically then enforce capacity
            self._evict()

    def _evict(self):
        now = time.time()
        # OrderedDict has no cheap tail-expired scan, so only check ends
        while self._data:
            _, (v, e) = next(reversed(self._data.items())) if False else (None, (None, float("inf")))
            break
        while len(self._data) > self.capacity:
            self._data.popitem(last=False)  # evict LRU

blocks.text: The Python version deliberately uses `OrderedDict` instead of hand-rolled pointers. Trade-off: in Java you prove you can maintain pointers under a lock; in Python you prove you know the standard library and that `pop` plus reinsert is O(1) promotion. Both keep the same contract: lazy expiry, single lock, eviction only from the LRU end. Note the Python lock is still required — `OrderedDict` is not thread-safe for the pop-then-insert promotion sequence, and two interleaved `get` calls will silently lose an entry or corrupt order without it.
Complexity

blocks.caption: Costs of the map-plus-list design.
rows: HashMap lookup plus constant pointer rewiring; lock acquisition dominates
One lookup plus optional unlink; no scan
One tail unlink per eviction; expired-tail sweep is bounded by evicted count
remove unlinks one node; clear must drop N nodes
One Node plus one map entry per live key; two pointers overhead per entry

blocks.text: Concurrency — the hardest follow-up

The lock choice is the whole Hard grade. A single `ReentrantLock` around map plus list is correct and fast enough to about 8-16 contending threads because each critical section is ten pointer assignments. Beyond that, promotion on every `get` makes it a write bottleneck — `ReadWriteLock` does not help since reads take the write lock anyway. The honest scaling path is sharding: N independent LRU segments keyed by `hash & (N-1)`, each with its own lock and capacity `total/N`. Trade-off: you lose exact global LRU — a segment can evict while another has slack — but you gain near-linear throughput and still bound total memory. Say that trade-off before they ask. The second concurrency trap is read-through thundering herd: 100 threads miss on the same hot key and all hit the database. Fix with singleflight — a `ConcurrentHashMap<K, CompletableFuture<V>>` of in-flight loads. First thread installs the future and loads outside the cache lock; others attach to the same future instead of loading. On completion, install under lock and remove the future. Never hold the cache lock during I/O, never call user loader code under lock, and always remove the in-flight entry in a `finally` or a second thundering herd forms on loader failure. If they push further, mention stampede guards: short negative caching of loader exceptions, per-key `tryLock` with fallback to stale value, and time-bounded futures so one slow load cannot pin 100 waiters forever.

blocks.title: Three ways candidates corrupt the cache
blocks.text: One, **promoting without the lock** because get felt read-only — two concurrent promotes interleave `prev/next` writes and the list permanently loses a node. Two, **calling the loader under lock** — throughput dies and a loader that calls `get` deadlocks on a non-reentrant path. Three, **using `System.nanoTime` deltas mixed with wall-clock expiry** — expiry must use one clock. Pick wall-clock millis for TTL and say why: TTL is a wall-clock contract, not a monotonic interval.
Follow-ups to have ready

items.title: Swap LRU for LFU or weighted size
items.text: Keep the map-plus-structure split. LFU needs map to frequency-node plus frequency buckets; weighted needs total weight counter and evict-until-fits loop. The lock boundary does not move.

items.title: Add read-through with singleflight
items.text: Add getOrLoad(key, loader) with in-flight futures map. Sketch the double-check: fast get, install future with putIfAbsent, load outside lock, put result, complete future.

items.title: Add write-through / write-behind
items.text: Write-through calls the store synchronously on put and fails the put on store failure. Write-behind queues dirty nodes to a bounded executor and risks data loss on crash. Name the durability trade-off.

items.title: Add statistics and events
items.text: Hit rate, eviction count, expiry count via LongAdder outside the lock. Eviction listener must be invoked outside the lock or after unlink with a snapshot, never reentrantly.

items.title: Shard for throughput
items.text: Fixed segment count, per-segment LRUCache, hash routing. Accept approximate global LRU. Mention consistent sizing: capacity must divide cleanly or one segment starves.

blocks.text: Edge cases to state unprompted

items: Capacity 0 or negative — reject at construction, not on first `put`.
`put` on existing key must update value and TTL and promote; forgetting promotion breaks every LRU test.
TTL already elapsed at `put` time — treat as immediate expiry; do not insert then instantly evict.
`null` keys or values — reject explicitly; `null` return from `get` already means miss, so storing `null` makes miss indistinguishable.
Clock skew and overflow — `currentTimeMillis + ttl` can overflow; clamp to `Long.MAX_VALUE`.
Expired entry still counted in `size` — either reclaim eagerly on write path or document that `size` triggers a tail sweep.
Reentrant loader calling back into cache — must not deadlock; loader runs lock-free.
Clear during in-flight loads — decide whether in-flight installs resurrect entries after clear, and state the choice.

blocks.title: 45-minute plan
blocks.text: Minutes 0-5: lock requirements table — capacity unit, LRU fixed, lazy TTL, single-process. Minutes 5-10: name why naive fails and draw map-plus-list. Minutes 10-30: write the Java core — Node, sentinels, get with promote, put with evict, one lock. Say each trade-off as you write. Minutes 30-40: handle TTL plus concurrency deep dive — why get takes write lock, load-outside-lock, singleflight sketch. Minutes 40-45: close with edge cases and sharding trade-off. If you are behind, drop the cleaner thread and statistics — never drop lock correctness.
